h1: Landscaping and grounds care in Colwood
cardSummary: Royal Bay and Latoria new builds beside older lagoon-side lots, with clear pruning limits under the Urban Forest Bylaw.
intro: Colwood splits between new neighbourhoods in Royal Bay and Latoria and older lots around Esquimalt Lagoon, Wishart and Colwood Corners, with Hatley Park’s woodland in between.

Colwood’s Urban Forest Bylaw is unusually specific about pruning: work that keeps at least half the live crown and removes no more than a quarter in a season does not need a permit, while removing a protected tree needs a Tree Management Permit. See [tree and vegetation work](/services/tree-vegetation/) or [request a free quote](/free-quote/?area=colwood).
localRulesIntro: Colwood draws a clear line between pruning, which is allowed within set limits, and removal, which needs a Tree Management Permit for protected trees. Native species are protected from very small sizes.

localNotes.title: Colwood Urban Forest Bylaw
localNotes.text: Colwood's Urban Forest Bylaw protects Garry oak, arbutus, Pacific dogwood and Pacific yew at 2 m tall or 4 cm diameter; Douglas-fir, grand fir, bigleaf maple and western redcedar at 30 cm; and any tree over 60 cm or identified as retained, replacement or wildlife tree. Removal needs a Tree Management Permit; pruning within stated limits (keep at least 50% live crown, no more than 25% removed per season) and some hedge work do not.

localNotes.title: CRD lawn-watering schedule
localNotes.text: CRD Stage 1 watering rules run May 1 to September 30 for properties on the regional water supply: lawns may be watered on Wednesdays and Saturdays (even addresses) or Thursdays and Sundays (odd addresses), 4-10 am or 7-10 pm; hand watering and drip irrigation of trees, shrubs and gardens is allowed any day. Multi-unit complexes use the complex's street address. New sod or seed does not need a permit and has a temporary schedule.

localNotes.title: Invasive plants and disposal
localNotes.text: The CRD Regional Invasive Species Program lists priority species (including giant hogweed, knotweed, gorse, poison hemlock, shiny geranium and yellow toadflax) and asks for sightings to be reported. Invasive plants must be disposed of properly: Hartland Landfill takes them bagged and labelled or in covered loads, and knotweed needs a controlled waste permit and is not accepted at municipal yard-waste drop-offs.

conditions.title: Fresh builds in Royal Bay and Latoria
conditions.body: New yards are often bare, compacted subsoil after construction. Grading, soil and drainage come first, or patios settle and lawns stay patchy.

conditions.title: Lagoon and Strait exposure
conditions.body: Lots near Esquimalt Lagoon and along the Royal Bay shore take wind off the water, so planting there needs to be wind-firm and salt-tolerant.

conditions.title: Native trees on older lots
conditions.body: Older Colwood lots often keep Douglas-fir, Garry oak and arbutus. With oak and arbutus protected from 2 m tall, even young native trees deserve a check before they come out.

topServices.why: Many new-build owners want the bare yard finished: grading, a patio, a retaining wall and planting.
The bylaw’s pruning limits let a lot of tree work proceed without a permit, as long as it is done within them.

jobNotes.title: Second-year lawn rescue
jobNotes.body: Builder sod that had thinned over compacted fill was aerated and top-dressed in its second spring instead of being replaced.

jobNotes.title: Driveway clearance inside the limits
jobNotes.body: Lower limbs on a Douglas-fir over a driveway were lifted while keeping well over half the live crown, inside the bylaw’s no-permit pruning limits.
